papers.title: Bourgain's Theorem for a Union of Euclidean Metric Spaces
papers.abstract: We study the distortion of embedding a union of $k$ Euclidean sets into Euclidean space. We show that a union of $k$ Euclidean sets can be embedded with distortion at most $O(k^{1.128} \log k)$, independent of the number of points. This is an exponential improvement over the previous best known upper bound of $2^{O(k)}$ obtained by iterating the result of Makarychev and Makarychev (2016) for the special case $k = 2$. Surprisingly, with the additional assumption that each Euclidean set remains Euclidean when we adjoin any other two points, we can obtain an asymptotically tight distortion of $O(\log k)$, thus, providing a generalization of Bourgain's Theorem (1985). Along the way, we also show that the distortion of the union can be upper bounded by $O(\log k)$ times the maximum of the Lipschitz extension constants of individual Euclidean sets.

papers.title: Greedy Byte-Pair Encoding Achieves at Least 0.361 of the Optimal Compression
papers.abstract: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) builds a tokeniser by repeatedly merging a most frequent adjacent pair of symbols; its utility is the total reduction in string length achieved by $k$ merges. It was known that this greedy rule achieves at least a third of the optimal reduction. We prove that it always achieves at least 0.361 of the optimal reduction in string length, for every string, every budget and every tie-breaking rule; this is the first improvement of the bound one third. We also explain why one third was a barrier: the pair-packing relaxation behind it is tight, so a better bound must use more of the optimum's structure. When greedy destroys three of the optimum's merge points at once, one of them can usually be moved next door, because all copies of a rule of the optimum look alike; the remaining cases are paid for later. Along the way we determine the worst-case ratio for two merges exactly, bound it for three, and isolate a single inequality that would settle the problem.

papers.title: On Differentially Private Mechanisms for Linear Regression
papers.abstract: We study the classic least-squares linear regression problem under differential privacy (DP) in the batch and the continual observation setting. In the latter setting, the mechanism receives a stream of $n$ data points $(x_i,y_i)$ ($x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $y_i\in\mathbb{R}$) and must output an estimate of the optimal parameters at each time step $i$. Although differentially private linear regression has been extensively studied in the batch setting, the problem remains underexplored for the continual setting, with prior work being restricted to constrained linear regression and update time polynomial in $n$. In this work, we introduce ContinualAdaSSP, the first mechanism for unconstrained linear regression under continual differential privacy. Our mechanism's suboptimality gap is proportional to $\sqrt{d}\operatorname{polylog}(n)$. It requires $O(d^2\log{n})$ space and $O(d^2\log{n}+d^{\omega})$ update time, where $d$ is the dimension of the input space. We also study fundamental limits of differentially private linear regression by showing the first lower bounds for the box-constrained least-squares linear regression problem. Our lower bounds are proportional to $\min(n,\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\log^{1.5}d})$ for $(1,O(\frac{1}{n}))$-DP, and $\min(n,\frac{d}{\epsilon})$ for $\epsilon$-DP, and are derived using a reduction from a fingerprinting code problem from [Peter et al., 2024], providing new insights into the inherent hardness of this canonical task. Our experimental evaluation on real-world datasets shows that the accuracy of our continual observation mechanism clearly outperforms any other known differentially private mechanism for this problem such as rerunning the batch algorithm at each time step.

papers.title: PaB-tree: Parallel B+-tree with Batch Updates
papers.abstract: The B+-tree is a ubiquitous search index due to its provable I/O (cache) efficiency. Yet unlike batch-parallel binary search trees, which are both fast and widely available, no batch-parallel B+-tree offers strong empirical performance together with provable, near-optimal I/O efficiency. Prior B+-tree-based designs are either parallel but purely theoretical, with no high-performance implementation, or concurrent indexes such as the Bw-tree and Masstree, which run an order of magnitude slower on batch updates. We present PaB-tree, the first batch-parallel B+-tree with guarantees on work, span, and cache complexity alongside strong practical performance. Its core challenge -- repairing node overflows and underflows without eroding the tree's I/O advantage -- is resolved by one simple invariant: a repair never touches a sibling and is always pushed to the parent. A Promote primitive reduces batch construction and insertion to repeated node promotion, and batch deletion to reinsertion. Batch updates take O(B log_B n) work and O(log_B n) I/O per element, matching the sequential B+-tree bounds, with polylogarithmic span. Against highly-optimized parallel and concurrent baselines, PaB-tree delivers the best overall performance trade-off: up to 1.4x faster on construction and up to 3.6x faster on batch insertion than the strongest baseline, while preserving B+-tree query efficiency.

papers.title: Precedence Constraint Scheduling on a Fixed Number of Machines
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic exact algorithm for $P_m\mid\mathrm{prec},p_j=1\mid C_{\max}$ for every fixed $m\ge3$. The algorithm constructs an optimum schedule in $$ O(L)+m^{O(m^2)}\, n^{6m^2+13m+1} \, {\log n} $$ elementary RAM operations, where $n \ge 2$ is the number of jobs and $L$ is the binary input length. Its word size is $O(m^2 \log n)$ bits. An implementation with a fixed number of tapes uses $O(L)+m^{O(m^2)} \, n^{12m^2+26m+2} \, \log^3 n$ steps. For three machines the respective polynomial degrees are $94$ and $188$, apart from the displayed logarithmic factors.

papers.title: Improved Approximation and Hardness Bounds for $\beta$-TSP
papers.abstract: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) asks for a minimum-length Hamiltonian cycle in a complete weighted graph. Its approximability depends on the edge lengths: unrestricted instances admit no constant-factor approximation unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, metric instances admit Christofides' $3/2$-approximation, and fixed-dimensional Euclidean instances admit a PTAS. We study $\beta$-TSP, where the edge lengths satisfy $ \ell_{uw}\leq\beta(\ell_{uv}+\ell_{vw}) \qquad \forall\,u,v,w\in V\ \text{pairwise distinct}, \quad \beta\in\left[\tfrac{1}{2},1\right]. $ The condition arises naturally in various settings, for example, when metric travel times are combined with positive service times at the vertices. The previous best approximation algorithm, due to B\"ockenhauer et al., ranges from $1$ at $\beta=1/2$ to $3/2$ as $\beta$ approaches $1$. We obtain a strictly better guarantee for every $1/2<\beta<1$ by combining two simple constructions whose guarantees counterbalance each other. We also improve the best known approximation hardness bound for every $1/2<\beta<1$.

papers.title: Coresets for Capacitated Clustering via Dual Concentration
papers.abstract: We study coresets for clustering problems, focusing on the classical $k$-median and $k$-means objectives. A coreset is a small weighted summary of the input data that approximately preserves the clustering cost for every choice of centers. Such summaries are a central tool for scaling clustering algorithms to large datasets. In this work, we consider the capacitated setting, where the clustering is subject not only to choosing centers but also to respecting prescribed cluster-size constraints. This model is a natural generalization of standard clustering and has been widely studied, but its coreset complexity is less well understood. For finite metric spaces, we obtain optimal-size coresets; surprisingly, these match the best-known bounds for unconstrained clustering. We also give improved coreset bounds in Euclidean space, notably the first coresets with near-linear dependence in $k$ while being independent of the dimension and input size. The main new technical ingredients are concentration bounds for the dual solutions of min-cost flow problems, which allow for both significantly simpler and tighter analyses of the underlying sampling distribution used in the coreset construction.

papers.title: What remains of the planar induced minor conjectures?
papers.abstract: Dallard, Milani\v{c}, and \v{S}torgel, and independently Gartland and Lokshtanov, conjectured that for every planar graph $H$, Maximum Weight Independent Set and List $3$-Coloring are polynomial-time solvable in $H$-induced-minor-free graphs. As a structural explanation, Gartland and Lokshtanov further conjectured that such graphs admit balanced separators dominated by a constant number of vertices. Bonnet and Chang recently refuted the independent-set part of the algorithmic conjecture, by showing that Maximum Independent Set is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard in graphs excluding the $5\times5$ grid as an induced minor. We revisit both conjectures. We show that the graphs used by Bonnet and Chang exclude much simpler planar graphs, including several $16$-vertex trees, and we introduce a second, independent family of hard instances. We also prove that $3$-Coloring is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard in both settings, thus refuting the algorithmic conjecture in full, even in its quasipolynomial version, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{QP}$. On the structural side, we identify planar graphs $H$ for which the structural conjecture holds, while the algorithmic one fails. Thus, constantly dominated balanced separators cannot by themselves explain the tractability of Maximum Weight Independent Set and List $3$-Coloring.

papers.title: The k-Clique hypothesis is dead, for good
papers.abstract: We present an algorithm that solves the $k$-Clique problem for any large enough $k$ and any $n$-vertex graph in $n^{\left(\frac{\omega}{3}-c\right)k}$ time, where $\omega\geq 2$ is the matrix multiplication exponent and $c>0$ is a positive constant independent of both $\omega$ and $k$. This refutes the long-standing $k$-Clique conjecture, regardless of the value of the matrix multiplication constant, even if $\omega=2$. In fact, our algorithm solves the more general problem of counting weighted $k$-Cliques.

papers.title: Weighted and Unweighted Online Connectivity Augmentation via Geometric Hitting Set
papers.abstract: We study the Online Connectivity Augmentation Problem (OCAP) with cut arrivals. In this problem, we are given a $k$-edge-connected graph $G = (V,E)$ with $|V| = n$ and a set of links $L \subseteq \binom{V}{2}$. In each iteration, a minimum cut arrives to be augmented, and we seek to maintain a smallest set of links crossing all such cuts. This problem is a special case of online hitting set in which the ground set is $L$ and a sequence of sets to be hit arrive from $\mathcal{C} = \{\delta_L(C) : |\delta_E(C)| = k\}$. As such, OCAP admits a $O(\log^2 n)$-competitive algorithm using the classical algorithm for Online Set Cover of Alon, Awerbuch, Azar, Buchbinder, and Naor. If $k$ is odd, then OCAP reduces to the case where $G$ is a tree. This case was studied by Naor, Umboh, and Williamson, who gave an optimal $O(\log n)$-competitive algorithm, which even holds in weighted setting. Recently, Garg and Subramanian gave an $O(\log n)$-competitive algorithm for unweighted OCAP which holds in the popular node-arrival model, but not for cut-arrivals. No better than $O(\log^2 n)$-competitive algorithm is known for weighted OCAP. In this paper, we provide a nearly optimal $O(\log n \log \log n)$-competitive algorithm for weighted OCAP under cut-arrivals and an optimal $O(\log n)$-competitive algorithm for unweighted OCAP with cut-arrivals. We also give an $O(1)$ algorithm for Online Cycle Augmentation under node-arrivals. Since no $o(\log n)$-competitive algorithm is possible on a cycle with cut-arrivals, this establishes a separation between the best competitive ratio achievable in the two arrival models.

papers.title: Differentially Private All-Pairs Min Cut Values
papers.abstract: We study the problem of privately releasing the min cut values of all pairs of vertices in a given $n$-node weighted graph, under the edge-neighboring model. Straightforward application of advanced composition yields an approximate DP algorithm that outputs all min cut values up to $\tilde{O}(n)$ additive error. Prior works [Dalirrooyfard, Mitrovi{\'c} and Nevmyvaka, 2023; Aamand et al., 2026] have established that $\tilde{\Theta}(n)$ is the correct bound if the algorithm also needs to output cuts that realize the approximate min cut values. On the other hand, simply outputting the values could be an easier problem, but prior algorithms have been stuck on the $\tilde{O}(n)$ bound. In this work, we give an approximate DP algorithm outputting all-pair min cut values with $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ additive error, beating the linear error barrier. Our algorithm applies the sparse vector technique [Dwork and Roth, 2014] to maintain a hierarchical decomposition of the vertices based on the min cut structure. We also prove an $\Omega(\log^{3/2} n)$ lower bound for this problem.

papers.title: Optimal Contention Resolution from Samples
papers.abstract: Contention resolution schemes convert random sets which are ex-ante feasible for some constraint into sets which are feasible ex post, and their online variants have broad applications in Bayesian and stochastic optimization, including prophet inequalities and stochastic probing. In many such applications, however, full distributional knowledge is an unattainable requirement. This motivates the study of contention resolution schemes which employ a limited number of samples from the underlying distributions. We study sample-based contention resolution for $k$-uniform matroids, for both uniformly random and adversarial arrival orders, and compare their balance guarantees to the best possible with full distributional knowledge. For a single-item constraint, we show that one sample per element suffices for an optimal $(1-1/e)$-balanced ROCRS. For adversarial arrivals, however, we prove that no single-sample OCRS can be $1/2$-balanced, even for known arrival orders, separating contention resolution from prophet inequalities in the single-sample setting. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that two samples are necessary and sufficient for the optimal $1/2$ guarantee. We also present a single-sample $0.48$-balanced scheme. For general $k$, we give a simple single-sample ROCRS that achieves an optimal balance ratio of $1-e^{-k}k^k/k!$. In adversarial order, we obtain a single-sample $(1 - O(1/\sqrt{k}))$-balanced scheme, matching the optimal asymptotic dependence on $k$. Finally, we complete the picture by characterizing the minimum number of samples needed to match the optimal balance ratio achievable with full distributional knowledge. For random arrivals, one sample suffices for $k = 1,2,3,4$, and zero samples suffice for $k \geq 5$. For an adversarial arrival order, even known in advance, and any $k \geq 2$, we show that no constant number of samples suffices to achieve optimal balance.

papers.title: Adaptive Data Analysis and Adversarial Robustness on Insertion-Deletion Streams
papers.abstract: Classical streaming algorithms and statistical mechanisms frequently fail when future inputs or queries depend adaptively on prior outputs. In this work, we resolve central open questions in both adaptive data analysis (ADA) and adversarially robust turnstile streaming by introducing a unified hierarchical estimator-corrector-learner framework. For adaptive data analysis over an unrestricted domain, we design a randomized mechanism that answers $k$ adaptively chosen statistical queries to within additive error $\alpha$ using $\tilde{O}(\frac{\sqrt{k}}{\alpha} + \frac{1}{\alpha^2})$ samples, nearly matching the lower bounds of Hardt and Ullman [FOCS 2014] and Steinke and Ullman [COLT 2015] while improving upon the classic $\tilde{O}(\frac{\sqrt{k}}{\alpha^2})$ bound of Dwork et al. [STOC 2015] and Bassily et al. [STOC 2016]. For known finite domains $U$, we combine our mechanism with private multiplicative weights to improve the sample complexity to $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{\alpha^2}+ \min\left(\frac{\sqrt{k}}{\alpha}, \frac{\sqrt{\log |U|}}{\alpha^2}\right)\right)$. Building on our ADA mechanism, we construct a fixed linear sketch with a stateful decoder that answers $\tilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ adaptive $F_2$ moment estimation queries to within a $(1\pm\epsilon)$-multiplicative factor using $\tilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ bits of space. Finally, by embedding this sketch into a binary-tree recursion, we obtain the first nearly space-optimal adversarially robust algorithm for $F_2$ estimation on insertion-deletion streams. Our algorithm uses $\tilde O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ bits of space, improving upon the $\tilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^4})$ bound of Gribelyuk et al. [STOC 2026] and matching the insertion-only bound of Woodruff and Zhou [FOCS 2021]. This demonstrates that no asymptotic space overhead in $\epsilon$ is required to achieve adversarial robustness in the turnstile model.

papers.title: Online Bin Packing with Dispatch Deadlines
papers.abstract: We study a generalization of online bin packing by introducing dispatch deadlines. Items arrive over time in an online fashion. Each item has an arrival time, a size in $(0,1]$, and a deadline, all of which are revealed only when the item arrives. The algorithm must immediately and irrevocably assign the item to a unit-capacity bin that has not yet been dispatched. Each bin must be dispatched no later than the earliest deadline of the items assigned to it, and once it is dispatched, it cannot be used for future items. The goal is to minimize the number of bins used. Applications arise naturally in logistics. Additionally, the offline version of this problem has appeared under several names, including the clique partition problem in weighted interval graphs and the BinSchedule problem. This problem is also a special case of online bin packing with conflicts and is closely related to online bin packing models with delay costs. We study the competitive ratios of several classical online bin packing algorithms when applied to this problem, and show that a similar hierarchy of competitive ratios carries over. Our main technical results are that the competitive ratio of First-Fit is exactly $16/7 \approx 2.28571$, and that no deterministic online algorithm has a competitive ratio less than $11/5 = 2.2$, showing that First-Fit is quite close to best possible. In addition, Next-Fit and Worst-Fit have competitive ratio exactly $3$, and every algorithm in the Any-Fit class has competitive ratio between $16/7$ and $3$.

papers.title: As Easy as Rank One: Optimal Algorithms for Matroid Secretary and Single-Sample Matroid Prophet
papers.abstract: We resolve the matroid secretary conjecture in its strong form and the single-sample matroid prophet inequality problem, achieving competitive ratios $e$ and $2$, respectively. Both ratios are optimal, even for rank-one matroids. For matroid secretary, our ordinal algorithm accepts the elements of the canonical optimum independently, each with probability $1/e$. It needs only the number of elements in advance and uses an expected polynomial number of independence queries on arrived elements. For single-sample matroid prophet inequalities, our algorithm uses one sample per independent value distribution and $O(n^2)$ independence queries on a known $n$-element matroid. It works for every arrival order fixed independently of the samples, values, and algorithmic randomness. The selected elements and their values have exactly the joint distribution obtained by independently retaining each element--value pair in the canonical optimum of a fresh product draw with probability $1/2$. Our main algorithms maintain a reference state whose greedy solution contains every accepted element. Its updates, made even after rejections, preserve exact distributional invariants. A short reversible-update argument gives a $4$-probability-competitive secretary algorithm, already resolving the original conjecture; a related invariant gives the optimal single-sample prophet inequality. For secretary, we characterize the distributions achievable by ordinal algorithms through a finite polytope. A continuous-time formulation then lets us design an accepted-set distribution achieving the optimal ratio $e$ and realize it efficiently. We also obtain guarantees for matroid intersections.

papers.title: Global Sinkhorn Convergence and Spectral Stability of Matrix Scaling
papers.abstract: We give a global spectral bound for the Sinkhorn--Knopp (SK) algorithm. Let $A$ be a row-stochastic nonnegative $n\times n$ matrix admitting a finite doubly stochastic scaling $B$. Define \[ g=1-s_2(B)^2>0, \qquad D=\min\left\{\|(u,v)\|_\infty: B=\operatorname{diag}(e^u)A\operatorname{diag}(e^{-v})\right\}. \] From the standard initialization, SK achieves total marginal $\ell_1$ error $\varepsilon$ in \[ O\!\left(\frac{D+\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon)}{g}\right) \] iterations. A scale-invariant potential contracts globally according to the spectrum of $B$. The linear dependence on $D$ is necessary in the fixed-gap regime: we construct strictly positive inputs with constant input and endpoint spectral gaps, $D=\Theta(n)$, and an $\Omega(n)$ iteration lower bound at error $n^{-2}$. Our upper bound gives $O(n)$ iterations on this family. We next give spectral certificates for scalability and short scaling distance. For a row-stochastic input $A$ with positive column sums $c_j$, set \[ K=\frac{\max_jc_j}{\min_jc_j},\qquad \sigma=s_2\!\left(A\operatorname{diag}(c)^{-1/2}\right). \] The input-only condition $\sqrt K\,\sigma<1$ certifies exact scalability and polynomial scaling distortion, with $D=O(\log n)$ for fixed $K$ and a fixed positive spectral margin. Given a finite scaling $B$, the weaker condition $\sqrt K\,\sigma s_2(B)<1$ gives the same structural bounds. With a constant endpoint gap, these bounds imply logarithmic SK iteration complexity. Boundary constructions show that the strict spectral inequalities cannot uniformly be replaced by nonstrict ones.

papers.title: On the Communication Complexity of Shortcut Set Computation
papers.abstract: A recent breakthrough of Kogan and Parter (SODA '22) provided the first polynomial improvement in decades on the size/diameter tradeoff available for shortcut sets. However, algorithmic applications of shortcut sets have mostly not taken advantage of these new bounds. A barrier is that many shortcut set applications occur in \emph{decentralized} settings, and we generally lack decentralized algorithms implementing the Kogan-Parter bounds. To this end, we study the \emph{communication complexity} of constructing Kogan-Parter shortcut sets. The edges of an $n$-node directed graph are split between two players, Alice and Bob, who are also given a target diameter $D$. Our main result is a protocol that, for $D \le n^{1/3}$, allows Alice and Bob to agree on a shortcut set matching the Kogan-Parter tradeoff between size and diameter, while exchanging only $\Oish(n^2 / D^2)$ bits of communication. We also provide (non-matching) lower bounds on the communication complexity required to find a correct $D$-diameter shortcut set of any size. The main technical ingredient for the upper bounds is a low-communication protocol for finding a \emph{path cover}, a common subroutine in shortcut set constructions that has attracted some independent interest. Our protocol crucially avoids applications of Menger's theorem or antichain decompositions, as often done in prior work. On the lower bounds side, we relate the communication complexity of the shortcut set problem to the size of bridge-free path systems.

papers.title: Vertex Deletion on $H$-Induced-Minor-Free Graphs: Subexponential FPT Algorithms and Approximation Schemes
papers.abstract: We study vertex-deletion problems on string graphs and, more generally, on graphs excluding a fixed graph as an induced minor. For every fixed graph $H$, fixed nonnegative integer $t$, and fixed monadic second-order formula $\phi$, we consider the problem of finding a minimum-cardinality set $S$ such that $G-S$ has treewidth at most $t$ and satisfies $\phi$. This captures classic problems such as Vertex Cover, Feedback Vertex Set, and deletion to graphs of any fixed bounded treewidth. We give an algorithm with running time $2^{k^{2/3} \log^{O(1)} k}n^{O(1)}$ on $H$-induced-minor-free graphs, where $k$ is the optimum deletion-set size. This resolves in the affirmative the open problem highlighted by Bonnet and Rz\k{a}\.{z}ewski [Algorithmica 2019] and Berthe, Bougeret, Gon\c{c}alves, and Raymond [ICALP 2025] regarding the existence of a subexponential parameterized algorithm for Feedback Vertex Set on string graphs. Our algorithm significantly improves over existing parameterized algorithms for more restricted classes of problems on more restricted classes of graphs. When the property defined by $\phi$ is hereditary, we also obtain a quasi-polynomial time approximation scheme, namely an algorithm that produces a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate solution in quasi-polynomial time. Both the sub-exponential algorithm and the quasi-polynomial time approximation scheme build on the same new structural and algorithmic insights.

papers.title: Load Balancing with Item Fragmentation and More Bins than Items: Linear-Time and Exact
papers.abstract: We study a fundamental load-balancing problem in which $N$ items of strictly positive integer sizes with total size $W$ must be assigned to $B$ bins, with items allowed to be divided into integer-size fragments across bins. Each bin must receive a load of either $\lfloor W/B \rfloor$ or $\lceil W/B \rceil$, ensuring that the loads of any two bins differ by at most one unit. Under this constraint, the objective is to minimize the maximum number of distinct item fragments placed into any single bin. This problem is NP-hard and there exists an $(\mathrm{OPT}+1)$-approximation algorithm that runs in $O(N \log N + B)$ time [Kobert et al., 2014]. The existing algorithm is employed by several widely used production codes for phylogenetic reconstruction. Here, we focus on the case $B \ge N$, that is, bins are at least as numerous as items. This setting arises pervasively in modern parallel and distributed systems, as well as in iterative algorithms that rebalance their workload at every step. In this context, bins are machines or machine cores, and items represent computational tasks (jobs). Our central contribution is a remarkably simple $O(N)$-time algorithm that computes an optimal assignment in this setting; this assignment is encoded using $O(N)$ space. In particular, we prove that an optimum always exists in which every bin receives at most two fragments and provide a characterization of when one fragment per bin suffices. Our result strictly improves the $(\mathrm{OPT}+1)$-approximation of Kobert et al. in the many-bins setting and, together with it, yields a strongly polynomial-time $(\mathrm{OPT}+1)$-approximation algorithm for the general setting, as it removes the dependency on the number $B$ of bins.

papers.title: Tight Variable-Occurrence Bounds and Exponential Separations for Moser--Tardos and WalkSAT on 3-CNF
papers.abstract: We establish a sharp variable-occurrence threshold for polynomial expected-time convergence for the Moser--Tardos algorithm and the pure random-walk WalkSAT on 3-CNF formulas. For every formula with $m$ clauses and at most two occurrences per variable, both algorithms terminate in $O(m)$ expected updates. This occurrence bound is sharp: we construct an infinite family with at most three occurrences per variable on which both algorithms require $2^{\Theta(\sqrt{m})}$ expected updates. Surprisingly, this dynamical transition occurs strictly below the classical NP-completeness threshold at variable-occurrence degree four. We further establish exponential separations between the two algorithms on satisfiable 3-CNF formulas. On one family, WalkSAT terminates in $O(m^4)$ expected flips, whereas MT requires $2^{\Omega(m)}$ expected resampling steps. On another, MT terminates in $O(m)$ expected resampling steps, whereas WalkSAT requires $2^{\Omega(m)}$ expected flips. These constructions exploit the different ways in which single-variable flips and simultaneous resampling propagate local violations. Our results show that the algorithms' expected running times are incomparable even up to polynomial overhead on the same inputs.

papers.title: Pairwise Reconnection for Cost-Distance Steiner Trees
papers.abstract: The Uniform Cost-Distance Steiner Tree Problem asks for a rooted tree that minimizes the connection cost plus a weighted sum of root-to-terminal distances. We develop an algorithm that constructs two candidate trees: one based on direct connections to the root and another that pairs selected vertices and connects each pair to the root. The algorithm selects the tree with the smaller objective value. The resulting randomized algorithm achieves expected approximation factors of $1.698$ in the spanning case and $2.041$ in the general case, and it can be derandomized in polynomial time. The pairwise matching analysis charges part of the augmentation cost directly to the connection and delay costs of an optimal solution, rather than only to the separated lower bound used in previous analyses. This allows the $1.698$ factor to fall below the maximum multiplicative gap of $1+1/\sqrt{2}$ between the optimum value and that lower bound. We give instance families with approximation-ratio lower bounds approaching $1+1/\sqrt{2}$ for cut-and-reconnect algorithms that start from a minimum spanning tree and $3/2$ for the present algorithm. Finally, we show that the Uniform Cost-Distance Steiner Tree Problem and the Steiner-tree version of the Cable-Trench Problem are approximation equivalent up to an arbitrarily small additive loss.

papers.title: Additive $\Omega(\log^* OPT)$ Gap for Bin Packing with Three Items per Bin
papers.abstract: We prove that bin packing is NP-hard to approximate within an additive factor of $o(\ls\OPT)$, even when all item sizes are arbitrarily close to $1/3$. This gives the first lower bound for bin packing with an additive factor that depends explicitly on the optimum value. In addition, we give a polynomial-time reduction from any bin packing instance into one with item sizes arbitrarily close to $1/3$, preserving its additive configuration-LP gap up to constant factors. Thus, in the sense of additive configuration LP gap and up to a constant, we confirm the conjecture that 3-partition instances are the hardest bin packing instances. In particular, we obtain an unconditional $\Omega(\ls\OPT)$ gap for 3-partition instances. We build on the recent OpenAI construction that uses five items per bin and rules out any constant additive gap.

papers.title: Dual-Number Associative Arrays for One-Pass Provenance and Sensitivity
papers.abstract: Associative arrays and GraphBLAS express sparse computations as matrix operations over a chosen semiring, but the result normally contains only the ordinary value. We define a dual-number extension $D_k(S)=S\ltimes S^k$ that carries this value together with $k$ independent auxiliary channels in the same computation. We prove that the construction is a split square-zero extension of any commutative semiring. Over min-plus, the auxiliary value is the weight of the shortest walk constrained to use the corresponding edge, excluding the weight of that edge. This gives an exact shortest-path membership test for that edge, although ties return the union of the edges on all optimal paths. We implement the min-plus construction using sparse \texttt{python-graphblas} operations, with a fixpoint test that checks the value and auxiliary components together. We validate the implementation across 18,692 checks, including 2,825 tied target pairs. On random graphs with 100,000 vertices and 32 seed edges, the dual method is $3.39\times$ faster than the sequential algorithm but $1.50\times$ slower than a min-plus-specific batched method. This difference is largely explained by the dual method requiring $1.55\times$ as many sweeps. Thus, the main contribution is a general algebraic approach with competitive sparse performance, rather than information that specialized min-plus algorithms cannot already compute.

papers.title: A Fast and Accurate Algorithm for the $p \to q$ Norm of Sparse Non-Negative Matrices
papers.abstract: We present an algorithm that computes the $p \to q$ norm of a non-negative matrix with $s$ nonzero entries to accuracy $\varepsilon$ in time $\widetilde{O}(s^{3/2} \log (1/\varepsilon))$, for any $p \ge q \ge 1$. The fastest algorithm previously designed for this problem has running time $\widetilde{O}(s / \varepsilon)$ (Objois and Vladu, 2026), which is slower when high accuracy solutions are desired. Our algorithm employs a surprising application of Laplacian solvers inside an Interior Point Method (IPM). We formulate the problem as a linear optimization problem over a product of power cones, and show that the Newton updates of the IPM can be computed by solving a Laplacian system in a Schur complement after subtracting a rank-2 matrix. We also discuss an implementation of our algorithm, showing that it is practical and it outperforms optimized solvers such as MOSEK by factors of up to $20\times$ on a variety of tasks.

papers.title: Online Timely Bin Packing Revisited: A Simpler Algorithm with Optimality in Special Cases
papers.abstract: Online Timely Bin Packing is a variant of classical online bin packing in which items arrive over time with sizes and deadlines. Packing an item may be deferred until its deadline, but once a collection of items is packed into a bin, the bin is closed and cannot be used again. The objective is to minimize the total number of bins used. The problem was introduced by Khattar in 2023. In 2025, Aminian proposed Discrete-Greedy, a deterministic online algorithm with a competitive ratio of exactly $2$, which remains the best-known upper bound. Its analysis is particularly simple; however, the algorithm requires maintaining a fractional simulation internally and may leave usable space in some bins unfilled. We propose Thrifty-Greedy, a simple deterministic online algorithm that does not require a fractional simulation. We prove that its competitive ratio is exactly $2$, matching the best-known upper bound. At the same time, the algorithm automatically achieves the optimal competitive ratio on two natural classes of inputs: it is $1$-competitive when all items have the same size, and $1.5$-competitive when every item has size in $\{1/3,2/3\}$. In contrast, Discrete-Greedy has a competitive ratio of at least $2$ on both classes.

papers.title: Parallel Algorithms for Higher-Order Temporal H-Index Computation
papers.abstract: Ranking vertices by importance is a fundamental task in network mining. The H-index provides such a ranking by asking how many neighbors are themselves well connected; its higher-order temporal variant recursively applies this idea over time-respecting neighborhoods in temporal networks. Scaling its computation is difficult because the existing streaming algorithm intertwines temporal processing with H-index order, incurring maximum-degree-dependent costs and exposing little parallelism. We show that the temporal dependencies can instead be resolved once: each edge's time-dependent lookup is mapped to a fixed successor position, turning every H-index order into a parallel gather followed by a segmented suffix-H computation. Based on this reformulation, we derive a linear-work suffix-H algorithm, a parallel multicore CPU implementation, degree-adaptive GPU kernels, and a multi-GPU scheme that exchanges only distinct remotely queried states. Experiments on synthetic and real-world temporal graphs show that the reformulation alone is substantially faster than the streaming algorithm, and that GPUs add order-round speedups exceeding an order of magnitude over our multicore implementation on synthetic inputs with up to one billion temporal edges. On a 636M-edge Reddit network, eight GPUs compute 128 orders in 3.6 s of round time, whereas the streaming algorithm does not finish within an hour even at order 8.

papers.title: From Function Inversion to Preimage Reporting
papers.abstract: Given an arbitrary function $f:[N]\to[M]$, the function inversion problem asks to preprocess $f$ and to be able to, when given some $y\in [M]$, decide whether there exists some $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$ and if so, to report such an $x$. Recently, Fiat-Naor's solution to this problem has seen significant traction in theoretical computer science, and allowed for several conjectures related to meta-complexity and the 3SUM problem to be broken. In this paper, we consider the natural extension of the function inversion problem that we call preimage reporting. Here, instead of having to report only one $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$, the whole set $f^{-1}(y)$ must be found. We present a new general method to convert any arbitrary function inversion scheme into an efficient corresponding preimage reporting scheme. In particular, if $\Delta$ is the maximal indegree of $f$, we show that we can perform preimage reporting using space $S$ in time $T$ for any $T$ and $S$ satisfying $TS^2=N^2 \Delta$, matching a variant of a tradeoff obtained by Fiat and Naor for function inversion. This last result implies an improvement over the corresponding function inversion scheme itself, which constitutes the first function inversion scheme whose query time is inversely proportional to $|f^{-1}(y)|$. We derive new simple solutions for the $k$SUM-indexing with reporting and Jumbled indexing with reporting problems.

papers.title: Contention Resolution Against an Adversarial Scheduler
papers.abstract: In the classical contention-resolution problem, a set of players share a broadcast channel, and a player succeeds in a given time step if it is the only player to broadcast during that step. Implicit in the classical problem is the assumption that every player is free to act on every step: once a player arrives, it participates until it succeeds. We study what happens when that assumption is removed. In our model, an adversarial \emph{scheduler} decides, on each step, which subset of the players gets scheduled to participate in the step. An unscheduled player simply sleeps through the step. We measure a protocol by its \emph{efficiency}: the number of players divided by the expected number of steps in which at least one player was active. Our first result says that, so long as the players are given access to a global clock and to shared randomness, they can achieve efficiency $\Omega(1/\log n)$. The players are able to achieve this bound without requiring any channel feedback, and even if the adversarial scheduler is adaptive. We also give a matching lower bound of $O(1 / \log n)$, which holds even with channel feedback, and even for an oblivious scheduler. Our upper bounds all require the players to have access to a shared global clock and to shared randomness. Our final result says that this type of implicit shared state is necessary. If the players have neither a global clock nor shared randomness, then no protocol can achieve efficiency better than $O(\log n / n)$; and this holds even if the other aspects of the problem are designed to be as favorable for the players as possible (the channel gives ternary feedback and the adversary is oblivious).

papers.title: Quasipolynomial-Time Planning for Decodable POMDPs
papers.abstract: We study planning for finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with finite state, action, and observation spaces. Both exact and approximate planning are known to be computationally hard in this setting, so prior work has explored natural assumptions that make planning easier. Recent work [Golowich et al., 2022] gave quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for observable POMDPs. These are POMDPs whose observation channels satisfy an $\ell_1$-observability condition, but notably, no assumptions are required on the transition dynamics. In a similar vein, for every fixed $\rho>0$, we give quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for $\rho$-decodable POMDPs. We show that decodability is implied by both $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-observability and is strictly weaker than observability. Moreover, we show that the optimal decodability constant can be computed in polynomial time, whereas computing the optimal $\ell_1$-observability constant is NP-hard in the worst case. We also show that the fast filter-forgetting guarantee underlying the approach of [Golowich et al., 2022] does not extend directly from $\ell_1$-observability to constant $\ell_2$-observability. Thus, decodability is an easy-to-check, unifying assumption under which quasipolynomial-time approximate planning for POMDPs is possible.

papers.title: Simulating Gaussian boson sampling on graphs in polynomial time
papers.abstract: We show that a distribution related to Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) on graphs can be sampled classically in polynomial time. Graphical applications of GBS typically sample from this distribution, and thus quantum algorithms do not provide exponential speedup for these applications. We also show that another distribution related to Boson sampling can be sampled classically in polynomial time.
